title: Carbohydrates
short: Sugars (monosaccharides like glucose) are quick energy; polysaccharides store energy (starch in plants, glycogen in animals) or build structure (cellulose in plant cell walls).
trouble: Students think starch and cellulose are different kinds of molecule because people can digest only one. Both are chains of glucose; the different links between the units make the difference.

blocks.html: Bread, pasta, fruit, paper and cotton are mostly carbohydrates. They are built from the sugars you saw joined in Monomers and Polymers, and they contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

Monosaccharides (simple sugars such as glucose) are quick energy. Disaccharides are two sugars joined. Polysaccharides are long chains that store energy (starch in plants, glycogen in animals) or build structure (cellulose in plant cell walls, chitin in insect shells and fungal cell walls).

blocks.name: bi-molecule
blocks.cap: The four kinds of large biological molecules. Carbohydrates are chains of sugars.

blocks.html: Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. The difference is how the glucose units are linked. In starch, the links make the chain coil, and our digestive enzymes (amylase) fit those links. In cellulose, every other glucose is flipped, giving straight chains that line up side by side and hydrogen-bond into tough fibers. Our enzymes do not fit those links, so cellulose passes through us as fiber. Cows and termites digest it with the help of microbes that make the right enzyme.

blocks.title: Sort the sugars
steps: Fructose is a single sugar: monosaccharide.
Glycogen and cellulose are long chains: polysaccharides (glycogen stores energy in animals; cellulose builds plant cell walls).
blocks.a: Mono: fructose. Di: sucrose. Poly: glycogen, cellulose.

cards.why: A structural polysaccharide in insect shells and fungal walls.
Animals store glucose this way, in the liver and muscles.

blocks.html: Thinking starch and cellulose are different kinds of molecule because people can digest only one. Both are polymers of the same monomer, glucose. Only the way the units are linked differs, and enzymes are fussy about the shape of the link. Check: break either one completely by hydrolysis and you get nothing but glucose.
